headline: Bunker Stacking the Bay: Blues Feasting, Bass Still Staged, Fluke Thinning Fast
subhead: The bait's here in numbers we called last week — now it's a waiting game for the water to cool enough to flip the switch.
body_markdown:
This week the smart play is to work the bunker schools where they're thickest — the flats off Keyport running down toward Flynn's Knoll — and treat anything with fins under them as a bonus, not a guarantee. The bait's been piling in for two weeks straight, exactly the setup we flagged last week when the schools first started showing density in the bay. That call is holding: bunker are stacked thick from Keyport Flats out past Flynn's Knoll and around toward Romer Shoal, and the bluefish have found every pod of them. What hasn't happened yet is the full striper commitment, and the reason is simple — the water's still sitting in the low-to-mid 70s. That's warm enough to keep bass scattered and picky, hitting under the bait rather than exploding through it.

The moon is the thing to watch here. We're building toward full around September 6-7, and that means bigger tidal swings starting this weekend into early next week. More water moving through Chapel Hill and the reach off the Highlands will start squeezing these loose bunker schools into tighter, more nervous balls — and tighter bait means predators start feeding with less hesitation. If the pattern holds the way it usually does this time of year, the first real blitz activity in this bay is more likely to break in the next week to ten days than this weekend, but the pieces are lining up fast. Keep gear rigged and ready, because when this bay flips from staged to committed, it can happen inside of one tide.

Bluefish are the dependable story right now, and dock talk up and down the Amboy and Keyport waterfront backs that up — this is the most consistent bite in the system. Snag-and-drop off live bunker is producing chopper blues to 8-10 pounds around Flynn's Knoll and the deeper edge off Romer Shoal, especially on the last two hours of the incoming when the current stacks bait against the shoal itself. Diamond jigs, half-ounce to two-ounce depending on the drift speed, worked with a jigging motion through the middle of the bait balls, are also connecting well for boats not wanting to mess with snagging gear. If you're marking bait on the sounder in 15 to 25 feet anywhere between the Knoll and the Hook, there's a good chance blues are underneath it.

Stripers are there, but call this a staged bite, not a blitz. The fish are sitting under and around the bunker pods rather than working through them, which means the best presentations are ones that put bait right in their face rather than counting on a surface eruption to find them. Bunker chunks fished on fish-finder rigs, 3-ounce sinkers, right along the bottom edges of the Chapel Hill Channel and around the mouth of the Navesink have been picking off keeper-class bass in the 26 to 32 inch range, mostly on the tail end of the outgoing when the current slows enough for the chunks to sit still. Live bunker on a circle hook, drifted just off the bottom near the Knoll on slack tide into the start of the flood, has also been worth the trouble for boats patient enough to wait out slow bites. The Shrewsbury and Navesink rivers are both holding bait and should be on the list for evening trips — weakfish have been mixed in on the dusk bite in the deeper holes off the Highlands side, though numbers are light and this is more a bonus fish than a target right now.

Fluke are winding down, and this is the part of the report where honesty matters more than hype. The doormat run through the back bays and inlet structure is basically over for the season — those big females have already started sliding out toward ocean-side structure ahead of the fall migration, and the numbers left in the bay are thinning fast. That said, there's still quality fish being pulled off the channel edges for anglere willing to work them properly. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along the drop-offs where Keyport Flats spills into the main channel, in 20 to 30 feet of water on the outgoing tide, are still turning up fish in the 3 to 5 pound range. It's not the volume bite of June and July anymore — treat every keeper fluke this week as a good one, because the window on numbers is closing.

Looking at the next few days: expect winds and tides to behave close to what we've seen, with the building moon steadily increasing current strength through the weekend. That's good news for concentrating bait and bad news for anyone hoping for a lazy, easy drift — moving water is going to be the theme. If you only have one window this week, fish the last two hours of the incoming around Flynn's Knoll or Romer Shoal, when the tide is pushing hardest and the bait gets pinned against structure. That's where the blues are most reliable and where the staged bass are most likely to finally commit. Keep an eye on overnight air temps — the first real cool front of September is the piece still missing, and once that shows up alongside this building moon, this bay has the ingredients to go from a bait-and-blues story to a genuine fall bass blitz in short order.
